cards.title: Robert Richard Torrens
cards.body: Arrived 1840, became collector of customs on £350, spent the next decade in trouble — censured for unauthorised absence, sued successfully for false imprisonment, convicted of common assault. Colonial treasurer and registrar-general from 1852. Stood for Adelaide in 1857 on land reform, topped the poll, introduced the bill as a private member. He claimed authorship; many others helped.
cards.prompt: Getting the Act passed was the easy half. Name the two things Torrens did after January 1858 — neither of them drafting — that turned a statute into a system other colonies copied.
cards.answer: He resigned his seat to take the job: he became Registrar-General under his own Act at £1000 a year, and from 1858 to 1862 helped turn it into what the ADB calls a workable and working system, organising meetings and petitions. Then he sold it — travelling to the other colonies advocating adoption, and later lecturing on it in England, Scotland and Ireland. Writing the authority is not the work; operating it and getting everyone to point at it is.

cards.title: Pedulla v Panetta
cards.body: Teresa Pedulla was living with an order of nuns in Calabria. Her brother's manoeuvres produced a forged power of attorney and a forged authority, and in 2007 her property was transferred to him and his wife-to-be for a stated consideration of $1. Pedulla v Panetta (2011) 16 BPR 30,229.
cards.prompt: The register said the brother owned it, so he sold it, and the buyers knew nothing. Say what the court could not undo, what the state paid instead, and which of those two facts is the reason for the other.
cards.answer: It could not undo the sale. The buyers paid $3.8 million in April 2011 and kept the house, because the entry is what vests title and it does not get rewound just because the write before it was a forgery. So the true owner was paid instead: $3.8 million out of the state assurance fund, plus over $329,000 in costs. The brother and his partner left Australia in May 2011, netting over $684,000 each, and have not been seen since. The register's authority is exactly why the remedy had to be money.

cards.title: Real Property Act 1858 (South Australia)
cards.body: Section 31 is the whole idea: no instrument passes an estate in land until the Registrar-General enters its particulars in the book of registry. It also settles the race — two instruments from one seller for the same land presented "at the same time", and he registers the one whose holder produces the grant or certificate of title.
cards.prompt: Section 31 makes the entry, not the deed, the act that transfers land. But the Registrar-General can refuse to make any entry until something else exists first. What, and what is its equivalent in a matching service?
cards.answer: A canonical identity for the parcel. Section 115 lets him require a signed map or plan of the land, drawn to a stated scale, and if the owner will not deposit one then "it shall not be incumbent on the Registrar-General to proceed with the bringing of such land under the operation of this Act, or with the registration of such transfer or lease". You cannot claim what the register cannot name. The matcher's equivalent is the cell id and the single shard that owns the driver: the geospatial index has to exist before a compare-and-set on a driver means anything. Index first, lock second.

cards.title: The Assurance Fund
cards.sub: 1858 · still statute in all eight Australian jurisdictions
cards.body: Section 34 of the 1858 Act levied one farthing in the pound sterling on the value of land brought under it; section 35 paid that to the Treasurer to constitute an Assurance Fund, making good what a court awards the rightful owner, failing recovery from whoever became registered "by fraud, misrepresentation, or error".
cards.prompt: The chapter calls a lost Redis reservation acceptable and a lost trip row not. The colony made the same call in 1858 and put a price on it before anyone had registered a thing. What was the price, and what does paying it buy that a rollback would not?
cards.answer: A farthing in the pound — 1/960 of the land's value, charged up front on every parcel. It buys the register the right to be believed. Once the entry is the truth and the land has reached a buyer who paid in good faith, you cannot unwind it, so the only remedy left is compensation: Low and Griggs put it flatly, "Compensation is payable when a person is deprived of land or an estate or interest in land", and all eight Australian jurisdictions still statute a scheme, from the Land Titles Act 1925 (ACT) to the Transfer of Land Act 1893 (WA). Same shape as the chapter's answer on duplicate offers: bound the damage and pay for it, do not promise to undo it.
